scenes.tts: The neurons at the back of your cerebral cortex are as old as you are. How could anyone know that? A cell carries no birth certificate. Part of the answer came from nuclear bomb tests.
scenes.visual: A cortex neuron with a question mark where its birth date should be; a crossed-out birth certificate; then a bomb-test tag appears.

scenes.tts: Carbon fourteen is made at a nearly steady rate in the upper atmosphere. Then came above-ground nuclear weapons tests. At their height, between nineteen fifty-five and nineteen sixty-three, they nearly doubled the level in northern hemisphere air. After the treaty of nineteen sixty-three banned tests in the atmosphere, the level fell year by year.
scenes.visual: A flat line grows into a peak then falls, drawn year by year on a computed curve.
scenes.caption: Carbon-14 is made at a nearly steady rate in the upper atmosphere. Then came above-ground nuclear weapons tests. At their height, between 1955 and 1963, they nearly doubled the level in northern hemisphere air. After the 1963 treaty banned tests in the atmosphere, the level fell year by year.

scenes.tts: Plants fix that carbon dioxide. People eat the plants, or animals that ate them. The carbon ends up in the DNA of every cell that divides. So each new cell records the carbon fourteen level of that year.
scenes.visual: Air, plant, animal and person, then a dividing cell whose DNA bar fills to the level of the air that year.

scenes.tts: Now think about a neuron. A neuron that has stopped dividing never copies its DNA again. So its DNA keeps the carbon fourteen of its birth year. Researchers sorted nuclei from post-mortem brain into neurons and other cells. Neurons of the occipital cortex were as old as the person. The other cells were younger. A sample holds many nuclei, so the value is an average.
scenes.visual: Neuron DNA gauge stays at the birth-year level on the curve; sorted nuclei: neurons match birth year, other cells land later; a mix collapses to one average.

scenes.tts: What about the hippocampus? One carbon fourteen estimate, from twenty thirteen, was that about one third of neurons there are subject to exchange. That is about seven hundred new neurons per day. Then two groups looked for young neurons in human tissue. In twenty eighteen, one group reported that none were detected in adults aged eighteen to seventy-seven. The next month, another reported thousands in healthy people aged fourteen to seventy-nine. The question is still argued over.
scenes.visual: Dentate gyrus arc with a third of its dots swapped; then two equal panels, one with no young-neuron stain and one with many.
scenes.caption: What about the hippocampus? One carbon-14 estimate, from 2013, was that about one third of neurons there are subject to exchange. That is about 700 new neurons per day. Then two groups looked for young neurons in human tissue. In 2018, one group reported that none were detected in adults aged 18 to 77. The next month, another reported thousands in healthy people aged 14 to 79. The question is still argued over.

scenes.tts: Why would careful laboratories disagree? The arguments are about method. The stain for young neurons weakens with time after death, so a missing signal may mean the marker was lost. It is also debated whether the markers label only newborn neurons. The carbon fourteen estimate rests on assumptions, including a turnover model. A fair statement is that the evidence does not yet settle it. So ask what a study can show, and what it cannot.
